Bug_Details:
Shift by an amount that is out of range For shift operations on int types, only the five lowest-order bits of the shift
amount are used as the shift distance. This means that shift amounts that are
not in the range 0 to 31, inclusive, are silently mapped to values in that
range. For example, a shift of an int by 32 is equivalent to shifting by 0,
i.e., a no-op. See JLS 15.19, “Shift Operators”, for more details.
Bug_Explanation: The bug is demonstrated by shifting an int by an amount that is out of range, specifically by 32. In Java, this is equivalent to shifting by 0 due to the way shift operations work with only the five lowest-order bits, resulting in a no-op instead of the intended shift.
Trigger_Explanation: The generated JUnit test cases trigger the bug by shifting the integer 1 by 32 and a negative value, both of which are out of range for int shifts. In the case of shifting by 32, the operation results in a no-op as Java interprets it as shifting by 0. Similarly, shifting by a negative value is handled improperly and results in unexpected behavior.
